title: How Tech Learned to Love the State
author: Geoff Shullenberger
content:
![How Tech Learned to Love the
State](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-28-at-7.30.50

>  _The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy_  
>  By Gil Duran  
> Avid Reader, 352 pages, $30  
>  
>  _Cyberlibertarianism: The Right-Wing Politics of Digital Technology_  
>  By David Golumbia  
> Minnesota, 480 pages, $34.95  
>  
>  _The Technological Republic: Hard Power, Soft Belief, and the Future of the
> West_  
>  By Alex Karp and Nicholas Zamiska  
> Crown Currency, 320 pages, $30  
>  
>  _Gilded Rage: Elon Musk and the Radicalization of Silicon Valley_  
>  By Jacob Silverman  
> Bloomsbury, 352 pages, $30  
>  
>  _Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed_  
>  By Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff  
> Harper, 242 pages, $30  
>  
>  _The Philosopher in the Valley: Alex Karp, Palantir, and the Rise of the
> Surveillance State_  
>  By Michael Steinberger  
> Avid Reader, 292 pages, $32.50

Of all the signs of the "vibe shift" that reverberated across America when
Donald Trump returned to power, the much-photographed presence of nearly every
major tech industry grandee near the inaugural dais last January was perhaps
the most striking. More than any other major American business sector, tech
had overwhelmingly backed Democrats for three decades. In 2016, when Trump
first ran for office, 80 percent of tech CEOs donated to Hillary Clinton and
her aligned PACs, and from the industry's employees, Clinton received $60 for
every dollar given to Trump. A 2017 survey of 600 tech elites found that just
8 percent of them had voted for Trump the prior year. Regardless of how many
of the CEOs present at the 2025 inauguration had actually pulled the lever for
or donated to Trump, they were eager to give the impression they had.

> "How exactly to interpret Silicon Valley's rightward shift remains open to
> debate."

How exactly to interpret Silicon Valley's rightward shift remains open to
debate. The explanations that have been proffered thus far fall into two main
categories. The first sort of account focuses on opportunistic alliances and
material incentives, while the second identifies the crucial factor in the
ideological commitments of the industry's leading figures. In its simplest
version, the materialist account notes that Trump is a uniquely transactional
politician, susceptible to flattery by other powerful people; having failed to
pursue the advantages of this approach during his first term, many tech
leaders decided to change tack. This narrative is accurate enough as far as it
goes, but fails to explain why an industry that long sold itself as more
idealistic than pragmatic suddenly became unabashed about cutting deals.

An answer to this question can be found in Jacob Silverman's book _Gilded
Rage_. The crucial background for understanding the mindset Big Tech leaders
brought into the current political moment, Silverman argues, was the end of
the "historical one-off" of post-recession zero-interest-rate policy (ZIRP).
During the 2010s, this unprecedented monetary regime flooded venture capital
firms with cash, and thereby "minted numerous millionaires and billionaires in
tech and finance, even when some appeared to produce little in the way of
public value or even viable businesses." ZIRP's suspension of the laws of
economic gravity fostered delusions of grandeur, prompting entrepreneurs to
present themselves more as philanthropic messiahs than normal businessmen. Its
abrupt end amid the pandemic-era inflation surge created an existential threat
to tech, to which no response could be too radical. "Rather than compete on
innovation and appeal to customers," Silverman says, the industry "would have
to bend government policy." And as its leaders realized, "Trump, for a fee,
would give them virtually anything they wanted."

The second sort of account of tech's rightward lurch, which foregrounds
ideology over material exigencies, can be found in Gil Duran's _The Nerd
Reich_. At the outset, Duran makes clear that "tech's embrace of Trump …
wasn't just about money." Instead, by lining up behind Trump, "the tech
industry revealed its true face." What was revealed in this mask-off moment
was what he calls "tech fascism," until then an underground ideology he
associates above all with Peter Thiel and his circle. Somewhat implausibly,
Duran presents Thiel as "the real power behind the throne" in the second Trump
administration, even though the investor steered clear of the 2024 campaign
and has spent much of the past year and a half delivering lectures on
theology.

Duran's polemical flair comes at the expense of analytical precision when he
tries to characterize the ideology of Trump-aligned tech leaders. Mussolini,
he explains, "sought to bundle every institution of Italian society under
unified state authority"--hence the term "fascism," from _fascio_ , meaning
"bundle"; comparably, he declares, "tech fascism bundles powerful technologies
… toward authoritarian goals." Of the many attempts to apply the f-word to
Trump and adjacent figures, this etymological red herring is particularly
unconvincing. Is the defining feature of fascism really "bundling" different
things together? Don't other sorts of regimes try to do this too? In his 1944
essay "What Is Fascism?" George Orwell enjoined his contemporaries "to use the
word with a certain amount of circumspection and not, as is usually done,
degrade it to the level of a swearword." Duran might have benefited from
following this advice.

 _The Nerd Reich_ inadvertently presents its readers with an enigma. Duran
focuses on exposing a worldview he regards as risible, yet he also suggests
again and again that its adherents have been stunningly adept at using it to
divine the future. For instance, he tells us that Thiel's thinking mostly
derives from the 1997 futurist tome _The Sovereign Individual_ , by the
investment gurus William Rees-Mogg and James Dale Davidson. The book, Duran
tells us, "is a work of zero academic merit produced by two men for whom dark
prophecy and lurid conspiracism became a mechanism for profit." And yet, he
informs us later, Thiel's "hopes and fears about the twenty-first century,
inspired by _The Sovereign Individual_ , have largely come to pass."
Similarly, Duran describes the "network state" theory of Thiel's fellow right-
wing tech investor Balaji Srinivasan--the idea that digital technology will
enable a proliferation of privately owned governments--as "stunningly
undercooked, offered with such conspiratorial self-certainty that you have to
wonder whether anyone has bothered to ask [Srinivasan] if he's alright." But
under Trump 2.0, Duran says, "the United States came to resemble a de facto
network state." How did ideas of such little merit prove so apt in their
prognoses, or else so efficacious as actionable political programs? So eager
is Duran for his readers to regard his subjects with withering disdain that he
forgets to explain to us how people in the thrall of such silly notions have
managed to use them as a "blueprint" to take over the world.

A no less denunciatory but somewhat more rigorous ideological expose can be
found in the late scholar David Golumbia's 2024 book _Cyberlibertarianism_.
Although Duran cites Golumbia, the latter's approach is quite different from
his. For Golumbia, "it is less the obvious, interested advocacy of right-wing
politics by openly libertarian figures like David Friedman, Peter Thiel, or
Eric Raymond that is of primary concern" than the way "the discourse of 'the
digital'" is "subtly embedded within broader right-wing ideology." What
defines this discourse, according to Golumbia, is the notion that "digital
technology is or should be beyond the oversight of democratic governments,"
which is the core tenet of "cyberlibertarianism" as he defines it. This view
has sometimes been presented by figures like Thiel, Srinivasan, and Curtis
Yarvin (Duran's main targets) as overtly anti-democratic in its implications.
However, as Golumbia documents, it has far more often been framed as enabling
a _superior_ form of democracy. Indeed, a great deal of left-wing organizing
in the first two decades of the twentieth century celebrated digital tools in
precisely these terms. A version of cyberlibertarianism has also been
enshrined in law; Golumbia cites, for instance, the principle that "code is
speech" and merits First Amendment protection as such. The implication of this
principle is that when it comes to tech, "governments cannot regulate what
corporations do," in effect placing technology beyond state oversight.

In the basic rhetorical modus operandi of cyberlibertarianism, Golumbia
argues, digital technologies--from e-commerce to social media to
cryptocurrency--are "claimed to promote freedom" and "cloaked in the rhetoric
of human rights." However, this rhetoric conceals the true objective: "the
freedom of a few … to skirt laws, regulations, rules, and institutional norms
that were put in place to protect people as individuals and as groups." Since
Golumbia's death in 2023, though, tech leaders have increasingly dispensed
with the first move--this is what the "mask-off" moment identified by Duran
amounts to. As I have [_argued_](https://compactmag.substack.com/p/attack-of-
the-zombie-cyberlibertarians), tech's continued appeals to cyberlibertarian
cliches are increasingly scattershot and incoherent. Industry leaders are now
more likely to argue for light regulation on national security grounds,
asserting that if America doesn't give its entrepreneurs free rein, China will
race ahead of us.

This is where Duran's claim that Thiel and his allies used _The Sovereign
Individual_ as an effective "blueprint" for governance in the new millennium
really falls apart. Rees-Mogg and Davidson's core prediction was that
decentralized network technologies would irreversibly weaken the power of
large, centralized nation states; the result, they argued, would be a sort of
universal balkanization, a fragmentation of states into smaller polities that
would compete to sell their services to mobile, wealthy, high-IQ "sovereign
individuals." Instead, as Thiel acknowledged in his 2020 introduction to a new
edition of the book, "the single biggest 'megapolitical' development since the
book came out" has been "the rise of China" as a "nationalist, ethnically
homogeneous, decidedly statist" superpower. Strikingly, given his reputation
today as an AI accelerationist hostile to state power, Thiel also wrote there
that "AI is communist," intrinsically favorable to the expansion of the power
of large centralized states, and might even "make it possible to centrally
control an entire economy."

Much of the tech industry seems to accept that a close alliance with the
national security state is the key to AI dominance; even crypto, the
technology Thiel counterposed in 2020 as the "libertarian" opposite pole to
"communist" AI, is now [entangled](https://www.compactmag.com/article/the-
real-reason-trump-backs-crypto/) with the federal government and monetary
policy under Trump 2.0, in an astonishing departure from its anti-state
origins. The main sense in which the current administration is realizing the
tech libertarian dream of privately owned government is in Trump's use of the
presidency as a lucrative branch of the family business--albeit not exactly in
the lean startup mode promoted by figures like Thiel, Srinivasan, and Yarvin.
Appropriately, Srinivasan recently relocated his "Network School" from a
Malaysian enclave adjacent to Singapore--long the tech libertarians' ideal
polity--to Kazakhstan, a notoriously corrupt petrostate. Actually existing
"private government," it turns out, may just be good old authoritarian
kleptocracy.

* * *

Tech leaders' strategic embrace of Trump will likely prove less significant in
the long term than the larger phenomenon of which it is a part: the
transformation of Silicon Valley's relationship to the state. From their early
adoption of Marshall McLuhan's "global village" as a positive aspiration to
the original utopian vision of social media as heralding a post-national
"community," the purveyors of digital technology saw themselves as
transcending the nation state and facilitating new forms of social
organization beyond its reach--even as they continued to be dependent on and
imbricated with state power in various ways. As Silverman shows, the end of
ZIRP forced a rhetorical and tactical shift. In effect, trading in the
language of openness and borderlessness for a more jingoistic register proved
a useful way to seek favorable regulatory treatment and public-private
partnerships for data center buildouts.

> "The end of ZIRP forced a rhetorical and tactical shift."

In their book _Muskism_ , Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff find the most
revealing case of the new "state symbiosis" paradigm in the career of the man
whose name provides the basis of their titular coinage. The book fuses the
material and ideological approaches. The authors treat the world's richest man
as an "avatar of a worldview," but locate this worldview less in Musk's
prolific tweets than in his business strategies and technological schemes.
Taken together, these constitute an "operating system for the twenty-first
century": a potential successor to Fordism and harbinger of new forms of
social organization to be implemented by corporations and states.

Unlike his sometime PayPal colleague Thiel, Slobodian and Tarnoff argue, Musk
was always guided by a "sense that governments were not something you should
try to escape altogether. In fact, they might provide the conditions for
profit-making," especially for contractors in rapidly privatizing sectors like
aerospace. Unlike during the Cold War, though, "design and production
decisions were no longer dictated by the state… Instead, entrepreneurs would
be the ones in charge." Companies like SpaceX would be reliant on government
contracts, but their innovation would be to make states ever more dependent on
them over the long term. The success of this gambit was made clear, for
instance, when Musk's Starlink reportedly found itself in the position to
dictate the course of the Ukraine war in September 2022. As Slobodian and
Tarnoff remark, "when a single individual owns the infrastructure, he doesn't
need to run a government to shape geopolitics." The short-lived DOGE project
looks, from this perspective, like a less successful effort to apply this
principle to federal bureaucracies, absorbing them into the operations of xAI.

_Muskism_ is effective at showing how, beneath his erratic and often deranged
public persona, Musk skilfully anticipated the new paradigm that has taken
hold in the 2020s--far more so than the figures highlighted by Duran. In
addition to fusing his operations with state power, Musk seems to have
intuited the waning of globalization. At a time when offshoring and diffuse
supply chains were still second nature to most businesses, he built Tesla
factories in the United States and emphasized vertical integration. Likewise,
he prioritized "hard tech" (cars, rockets, satellites) back when software was
supposed to be eating the world, presaging the booms in data center
construction and "new defense tech."

Slobodian and Tarnoff don't see the triumph of Muskism as foreordained,
arguing that we are now in a period of "institutional breakdown," that "at
some point, society will stabilize on a new basis," and that "Muskism could
provide the foundation." Looking beyond Musk's right-wing image, they suggest
Muskism is flexible enough to be taken in different ideological directions.
Henry Ford was no social democrat, but the political economy he helped usher
into existence "rewrote the social contract with a promise of rising living
standards for all." They don't offer much hope for a more egalitarian Muskism,
remarking that "it does not distribute rewards broadly," but they suggest that
under some conditions, "the Tesla ecosystem could materially improve people's
lives"--hinting at a potential return of Obama-era eco-conscious Muskism.

* * *

While other entrepreneurs were busy building mindfulness apps and delivery
platforms, Musk helped jumpstart the rebirth of Silicon Valley as a revived
military-industrial complex for a new era of geopolitical competition. He
isn't the only tech entrepreneur who managed to get ahead of this development.
Toward the end of _Muskism_ , the authors draw a comparison with Palantir CEO
Alex Karp, who is eager to tell anyone who will listen that he wants his
industry to "return to its roots as a Pentagon contractor, albeit in a more
sophisticated, nimble, and entrepreneurial form." In his 2025 manifesto _The
Technological Republic_ , published just as Palantir was ramping up its
military and intelligence work for the newly inaugurated Trump administration,
Karp declared that "the technology sector has an affirmative obligation to
support the state that made its rise possible" and decried the industry's
prior dedication to "chasing trivial consumer products."

> "Musk helped jumpstart the rebirth of Silicon Valley as a revived military-
> industrial complex."

Michael Steinberger's biography of Karp, _The Philosopher in the Valley_ ,
stands in contrast to _Muskism_ , even if it touches on many of the same
themes. Steinberger finds no "Karpism," only an idiosyncratic man whose
transformation into a leading representative of the tech industry during the
second Trump term pretty much no one could have foreseen based on his earlier
life. Unlike Musk and other peers, Karp showed no inclination at all to the
tech industry until his Stanford Law School friend Peter Thiel recruited him
to run Palantir. The selection was made, by all accounts, on the strength of
Karp's intelligence and forceful personality; it didn't hurt that, despite his
close association with Thiel, he described himself as a man of the left, which
would help the company market its services to politicians and officials of
varied political stripes.

Much has been made of Karp's intellectual
[background](https://www.compactmag.com/article/what-the-tech-right-learned-
from-habermas/) as an admirer and would-be doctoral student of the left-wing
German philosopher Jurgen Habermas, who declined to direct his dissertation at
Frankfurt's Goethe University; he ended up working under one of the _e minence
grise_'s students, Karola Brede. Karp's research topic, as Steinberger
recounts, was inspired by the resurgent debate about the Holocaust and
antisemitism in Germany prompted by the publication of Daniel Jonah
Goldhagen's 1996 book _Hitler 's Willing Executioners_. By Karp's own telling,
growing up dyslexic with a Jewish father and a black mother had attuned him
early on to the dangers of social exclusion and persecution, and his research
was driven by that abiding concern.

As Palantir's contracts with ICE and the IDF have become repeated flashpoints
of controversy, many have wondered at the fact that the company's CEO has this
personal and intellectual background. But Karp, by Steinberger's account,
seems unbothered by these supposed contradictions. "From the start," he
writes, "Karp said that Palantir's mission was to defend the West and liberal
democracy." His underlying worldview, informed by his upbringing and
philosophical studies, was informed by a deep pessimism about humanity's
tendencies to intolerance and violence. Protecting liberal societies, he
concluded, couldn't be done with kid gloves on. At various points, he argued
that effective counterterrorism was essential to preventing the rise of
illiberal populist parties, who could take advantage of real dangers to
exploit people's fears.

Karp is perhaps best understood as a Cold War liberal born in the wrong
generation. His career, and the twenty-some year history of Palantir,
illustrates the deeper point that the tech industry always remained deeply
imbricated with state power, even at the height of its libertarian rhetorical
appeals--as the Snowden leaks made plain well over a decade ago. _The
Technological Republic_ attempts to furnish an explicit ethos to a rising
technocratic elite that will oversee a new "union of science and the state."
As a precedent, Karp favorably cites Franklin Roosevelt's efforts, during
World War II, to "see that the machinery of the state … would spur the
scientific community forward in service of, among other things, the
advancement of public health and national welfare." Judging by the
increasingly incoherent but always aggressive anti-state rhetoric of other
Trump-aligned figures in the tech world, this approach remains a hard sell.
Most notably, Musk styled himself and his DOGE minions as outsiders and
"disruptors," rather than as pioneers of the sort of new "intimate
collaboration between the state and the technology sector" Karp advocates.

Karp and his co-author, Palantir legal counsel Nicholas Zamiska, present their
proposed collaborative enterprise as ideally cross-partisan, more structural
than politically substantive. As Tanner Greer
[_remarks_](https://americanaffairsjournal.org/2025/11/the-making-of-a-techno-
nationalist-elite/?ref=compactmag.com), the authors "demand a pulpit for
America's technologists but never summon the courage to state what gospel they
should preach." Perhaps they are keeping their options open for the post-Trump
future. But assuming the president's tanking approval ratings herald another
thermostatic shift in our political climate in the coming years, it isn't
clear that Karp will have much luck appealing to Democrats to take up his
proposed project of technocratic renewal. The bellicose rhetoric of his recent
public appearances has underlined his and his company's connections with some
of the current administration's most unpopular initiatives, which will likely
render him a toxic figure to most in the party he once supported.

What much of the Trump-aligned tech sector seems to want is state symbiosis--
in the form of government contracts, public-private partnerships, favorable
treatment for cryptocurrency investors--without even a pretense of democratic
accountability. As the surging backlash to such tech initiatives as data
centers and Flock cameras makes clear, the American public doesn't much like
that arrangement. Karp claims to want a more serious and durable pact between
state and industry, but as Greer argues, "elevating Silicon Valley's
engineering elite into a governing class would require much more" than what he
and Zamiska offer--specifically, "institutions, alliances, and traditions that
root the wealth and expertise of our technologists in service to the nation."
Tech's MAGA alignment may prove fleeting, but the merger of the tech sector
and the state will likely not. What is missing is a political project to
ensure that this fusion redounds to the public good.
